title: Given a list of words, find the longest word that can be built one character at a time, where every prefix of that word is also present in the list; break ties by taking the smallest word in dictionary order. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Word in Dictionary (Longest Word Buildable One Character at a Time)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Word in Dictionary is a traversal application of the Trie pattern. We insert every word into a trie, then run a depth-first search that only descends through nodes marked as complete words, because such a path means every prefix along it is itself a valid word. We keep the longest such reachable word, breaking ties by dictionary order. This runs in time proportional to the total characters.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, where each longer code must extend a code that already exists at every step. The bank wants the longest code reachable by adding one character at a time, which this finds with a trie.
s1_definition.oneliner: Only descend through nodes that are themselves words, and keep the longest reachable such path.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Word in Dictionary is a traversal application of the Trie pattern. We insert every word into a trie, then run a depth-first search that only descends through nodes marked as complete words, because such a path means every prefix along it is itself a valid word. We keep the longest such reachable word, breaking ties by dictionary order. This runs in time proportional to the total characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, where each longer code must extend a code that already exists at every step. The bank wants the longest code reachable by adding one character at a time, which this finds with a trie.

**One line to remember:** Only descend through nodes that are themselves words, and keep the longest reachable such path.

sections.s2_technical:
We insert all words into a trie, marking the end of each word. The key rule is that a word is buildable one character at a time only if every one of its prefixes is also a word in the list. In the trie that means a path is valid only if every node along it, below the root, is marked as a complete word. So we run a depth-first search from the root and only step into a child if that child is marked as a word, stopping a branch the moment a node is not a word.

As we descend we track the current string, and whenever we reach a node that is a word and the path is longer than the best so far, or equal in length but smaller in dictionary order, we update the best. We can get the dictionary-order tie-break for free by visiting children in sorted character order and preferring the first longest found. A concrete check: with words A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE the answer is APPLE because each prefix exists. Senior nuance: this is linear in the total characters, the word-only descent rule is what encodes the buildable constraint, and sorted child traversal handles the tie-break cleanly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, and a longer code is only valid if every shorter prefix of it is also a registered code, so the product team wants the longest buildable code, preferring the dictionary-smallest on ties. Checking every code's prefixes separately is wasteful. This is exactly how the Longest Word in Dictionary works: it uses the Trie pattern and a word-only descent to find the longest reachable code.

The code defines a `FeatureCodeService` with `longestBuildable(codes)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` inserts a small code set and logs the longest buildable code.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the code set A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE, B. We want the longest code whose every prefix is also present.

Step 1 — We build the trie, marking A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE as words along one branch and B as a word on another branch.

Step 2 — The depth-first search starts at the root and, visiting children in sorted order, steps into A first because A is a word, recording A as the best so far of length one.

Step 3 — From A it steps into AP because AP is a word, updating the best to AP of length two, then into APP, then APPL, each a word, extending the best each time.

Step 4 — From APPL it steps into APPLE because APPLE is a word, updating the best to APPLE of length five. There is no further word child, so this branch stops.

Step 5 — The search then considers B, which is a word of length one, but one is shorter than five so the best stays APPLE. The answer is APPLE. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 10:02:31 PM com.bank.featcode.service.FeatureCodeService longestBuildable
INFO: Longest buildable code = APPLE
Oct 27, 2026 10:02:31 PM com.bank.featcode.FeatureCodeApplication main
INFO: Longest incrementally buildable feature code: APPLE
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Build trie, mark words: A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE, B
    │
    ▼
  DFS from root, descend only into isWord children
    │ A(word) len1 → AP(word) len2 → APP len3 → APPL len4 → APPLE len5
    │ B(word) len1  (shorter, ignored)
    │ sorted children handle dictionary tie-break
    ▼
  Output: longest buildable = "APPLE"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Word in Dictionary is a traversal application of the Trie pattern, and the insight that makes it clean is that a word can be built one character at a time exactly when every one of its prefixes is also a word in the list. Once all words are inserted into a trie and each word end is marked, that condition becomes a simple structural rule: a path from the root is valid only if every node along it is marked as a complete word.

So I run a depth-first search from the root and only step into a child if that child is marked as a word, which stops a branch the instant a node is not a word. As I descend I track the current string, and I update my best answer whenever I reach a word node that is longer than my current best. I get the dictionary-order tie-break for free by storing children in sorted order and visiting them in that order, so among equal-length candidates the smallest is found first. The whole search is linear in the total number of characters.

At the National Bank of India I used this to find the longest incrementally buildable product feature code, where a longer code was only valid if every shorter prefix of it was also a registered code, preferring the dictionary-smallest on ties. I inserted the codes into a trie and ran the word-only descent. Explaining that the path-of-words rule encodes the buildable constraint, and that sorted children handle the tie-break, is what shows an interviewer I understand this traversal use of the Trie pattern.
